source.text: Ηὐφράνθην, φημί, κύριε, ταύτην τὴν ἐπίλυσιν ἀκούσας. Ἄκουε νῦν, φησί· τὴν σάρκα σου ταύτην φύλασσε καθαρὰν καὶ ἀμίαντον, ἵνα τὸ πνεῦμα τὸ κατοικοῦν ἐν αὐτῇ μαρτυρήσῃ αὐτῇ, καὶ δικαιωθῇ σου ἡ σάρξ. 2. βλέπε μήποτε ἀναβῇ ἐπὶ τὴν καρδίαν σου τὴν σάρκα σου ταύτην φθαρτὴν εἶναι, καὶ παραχρήσῃ αὐτῇ ἐν μιασμῷ τινί. ἐὰν [γὰρ] μιάνῃς τὴν σάρκα σου, μιανεῖς καὶ τὸ πνεῦμα τὸ ἅγιον· ἐὰν δὲ μιάνῃς †τὴν σάρκα†, οὐ ζήσῃ. 3. Εἰ δέ τις, φημί, κύριε, γέγονεν ἄγνοια προτέρα πρὶν ἀκουσθῶσι τὰ ῥήματα ταῦτα, πῶς σωθῇ ὁ ἄνθρωπος ὁ μιάνας τὴν σάρκα αὐτοῦ; Περὶ τῶν προτέρων, φησίν, ἀγνοημάτων τῷ Θεῷ μόνῳ δυνατὸν ἴασιν δοῦναι· αὐτοῦ γάρ ἐστι πᾶσα ἐξουσία. 4. [ἀλλὰ νῦν φύλασσε σεαυτόν, καὶ ὁ Κύριος ὁ παντοκράτωρ, πολύσπλαγχνος ὤν, περὶ τῶν προτέρων ἀγνοημάτων ἴασιν δώσει,] ἐὰν τὸ λοιπὸν μὴ μιάνῃς σου τὴν σάρκα μηδὲ τὸ πνεῦμα· ἀμφότερα γὰρ κοινά ἐστι καὶ ἄτερ ἀλλήλων μιανθῆναι οὐ δύναται. ἀμφότερα οὖν καθαρὰ φύλασσε, καὶ ζήσῃ τῷ Θεῷ.

translation.text:
“I rejoiced[i], Sir[a],” I say, “when I heard this explanation.”

“Listen now,” he says: “Keep this flesh of yours clean and undefiled, so that the spirit that dwells in it[c] may bear witness to it, and your flesh may be justified. Watch lest it ever rise up in your heart[b] that this flesh of yours is perishable, and you misuse it in some defilement. For if you defile your flesh, you will also defile the Holy Spirit; and if you defile the flesh,[d] you will not live.”

“But if, Sir,” I say, “there has been some former ignorance before these words were heard, how will the man who has defiled his flesh be saved?”

“As to former ignorances[f],” he says, “God alone is able to give healing concerning them; for all authority is his. But now guard yourself, and the Lord, the Almighty—being full of compassion—will give healing for former ignorances,[e] if from now on you do not defile your flesh or the spirit; for both are shared[g] and cannot be defiled apart from one another. Therefore keep both clean, and you will live to God[h].”

footnotes.text: Greek κύριε here is a polite address to the shepherd/angelic guide, hence “Sir,” not the divine title “Lord.”
“Rise up in your heart” is a Semitic-Greek idiom for “come into your mind” or “occur to you.”
“The spirit that dwells in it” may be understood as the human spirit or as the (Holy) Spirit; the Greek does not specify ἅγιον here. The explicit “Holy Spirit” follows in v.2.
The words “the flesh” in the second clause are textually uncertain (daggered in some editions). The sense is maintained either way: defilement leads to death.
Many editions bracket “But now guard yourself … will give healing for former ignorances,” as some witnesses omit it. It fits Hermas’ exhortational style; we include it here.
“Former ignorances” renders ἀγνοήματα, idiomatically “offenses committed in ignorance.”
“Both are shared” renders κοινά ἐστι as “held in common/partnered,” not “common” in the sense of “profane/unclean.”
“Live to God” mirrors the Greek dative (orientation). “Live for God” is an acceptable paraphrase.
Or 'Therefore keep both pure, and you will live to God[h].'.

lexical_decisions.rationale: Here it is a polite form of address to the shepherd/angelic figure, not the divine title. Rendering as “Sir” avoids confusion with “the Lord, the Almighty” later in the section.
In Hermas’ Similitudes the figure gives interpretations of symbols; “explanation” fits the context and preserves the technical sense without importing later theological jargon.
Hermas uses moral–ascetic language where ‘flesh’ carries ethical and purity connotations; “flesh” preserves that texture better than the neutral “body.”
“Clean” pairs naturally with cultic/purity imagery and with “undefiled,” echoing ritual purity language.
“Undefiled” is the standard purity term and keeps the moral-purity register.
The Greek lacks ἅγιον here; the identification is clarified in v.2. We retain lowercase “spirit” to preserve the textual ambiguity in v.1.
“Dwells” is idiomatic and keeps the indwelling nuance without sounding archaic.
“Bear witness” preserves the forensic/attestational nuance central to the clause.
Hermas frequently uses judicial language; “be justified” maintains that register and links with the witness motif.
A literal rendering keeps the idiom’s ancient texture; footnote clarifies the sense.
“Perishable” captures the susceptibility-to-decay nuance and matches the ethical warning that follows.
The verb denotes using wrongly; “misuse” is concise and clear in modern English.
“Defilement” preserves cultic-moral coloration consistent with Hermas’ purity concerns.
Standard moral-purity verb; “defile” keeps the traditional register.
Here the text explicitly names the Holy Spirit; capitalization reflects the title.
Retains the literal plural. A footnote clarifies the idiom as offenses committed in ignorance.
Hermas frequently frames repentance in medical terms; “healing” preserves the metaphor rather than flattening to ‘forgiveness.’
Title for God; comma retains appositional force; matches apocalyptic diction.
Idiomatic English equivalent of ‘much-compassioned’; aligns with James 5:11 usage.
Natural English expressing the temporal shift demanded by the exhortation.
Here ‘koinos’ means ‘shared/held in common,’ not ‘common’ in the sense ‘profane.’ “Are shared” communicates mutual participation of flesh and spirit.
Clear idiomatic rendering of separative sense.
Keeps the dative’s orientation (‘to God’) and the elevated tone; alternative noted in footnote.

theological_decisions.issue: Identification of “the spirit that dwells in it” (v.1)
alternative_readings: Render as “Spirit,” i.e., the Holy Spirit
theological_decisions.rationale: The Greek lacks ἅγιον in v.1, while v.2 explicitly names “the Holy Spirit.” Preserving the ambiguity in v.1 reflects the text’s progression and maintains tension between human spirit and divine Spirit.
Hermas consistently employs medical imagery for repentance and restoration. “Healing” keeps that metaphor active, while readers will naturally understand the soteriological sense.

theological_decisions.issue: Meaning of κοινά ἐστι (“both are κοινά”)
theological_decisions.chosen_reading: “Both are shared”—flesh and spirit are in mutual participation and cannot be defiled separately
theological_decisions.rationale: The point is the inseparability of moral defilement: body and (human/divine) spirit share in purity/defilement. Using “shared” avoids confusion with ‘common/profane’ while conveying the anthropology.
We retain the dative nuance and elevated tone, echoing the idiom of orientation toward God without over-smoothing.

theological_decisions.issue: Vocative κύριε addressed to the shepherd
theological_decisions.rationale: To avoid conflating the shepherd with God, and to reflect polite address to a superior/elder, we use “Sir.” Later “the Lord, the Almighty” refers unmistakably to God.

review_passes.summary: The draft is generally excellent and captures the moral and theological nuances well. However, it omits a few small words from the Greek (φημί in v.1; κύριε and τις in v.3). I have restored these and suggested a slight smoothing of 'Guard this flesh... keeping it' to 'Keep this flesh' to avoid adding a participle.
issues_found: Omission of φημί ('I say') in verse 1.
Addition of 'keeping it' in verse 1 to smooth 'Guard this flesh... clean'. Translating φύλασσε as 'Keep' allows a direct rendering without adding words.
Omission of κύριε ('Sir') and τις ('some') in verse 3.
Inconsistent translation of προτέρα/προτέρων as 'earlier' and 'former' in adjacent sentences.

revisions.from: Therefore keep both pure, and you will live to God[h].
revisions.to: Therefore keep both clean, and you will live to God[h].
revisions.rationale: The Greek word `καθαρὰ` is used here, which was translated as "clean" in verse 1 (`καθαρὰν`, "Keep this flesh of yours clean"). The lexical decision explicitly chose "clean" over "pure" to pair with cultic/purity imagery. Maintaining "clean" here preserves the author's lexical consistency and the inclusio of the paragraph. | Adjudicator: The author uses the exact same adjective and verb combination (καθαρὰ φύλασσε / φύλασσε καθαρὰν) at the beginning and end of this section to form a deliberate inclusio. Translating both instances of κ

base_translation.text: “Listen now,” he says: “Keep this flesh of yours pure and undefiled, so that the spirit that dwells in it may bear witness to it, and your flesh may be justified. Watch lest it ever rise up in your heart that this flesh of yours is perishable, and you misuse it in some defilement. For if you defile your flesh, you will also defile the Holy Spirit; and if you defile the flesh, you will not live.”

translation.text: He says, “Listen now. Keep your body pure and undefiled, so that the spirit living in it may testify for your body, and your body may be shown to be right. Never let yourself think, ‘My body will perish anyway,’ and use that as an excuse to defile it. If you defile your body, you will also defile the Holy Spirit. And if you defile your body, you will not live.”

simplification_decisions.preserved_meaning: The person’s physical body remains the object of the commands and warnings.
simplification_decisions.rationale: “Body” gives the contextual sense of “flesh” in familiar modern English.

simplification_decisions.pob_phrase: the spirit that dwells in it may bear witness to it, and your flesh may be justified
simplification_decisions.simplified_phrase: the spirit living in it may testify for your body, and your body may be shown to be right
simplification_decisions.preserved_meaning: The spirit may testify on the body’s behalf, with the result that the body may be justified.
simplification_decisions.rationale: This keeps the testimony unspecified and preserves the contingent force of both clauses.

simplification_decisions.pob_phrase: Watch lest it ever rise up in your heart that this flesh of yours is perishable, and you misuse it in some defilement
simplification_decisions.simplified_phrase: Never let yourself think, ‘My body will perish anyway,’ and use that as an excuse to defile it
simplification_decisions.preserved_meaning: The body’s mortality must not be treated as permission for impure conduct.
simplification_decisions.rationale: Direct-thought wording makes the warning and its logic clear.

interpretive_expansions.pob_phrase: and you misuse it in some defilement
interpretive_expansions.rendering: and use that as an excuse to defile it
interpretive_expansions.claim: The thought of bodily perishability becomes the grounds for defiling the body.
evidence: The warning directly joins the thought that the body is perishable with its misuse in defilement.
alternatives_preserved: The clause may describe consequence rather than a consciously stated excuse.

risk_flags.risk: Rendering “flesh” as “body” may soften the repeated source-language image.
risk_flags.mitigation: The physical focus and every warning about defiling the body remain explicit.

risk_flags.risk: The relation between the indwelling spirit and the Holy Spirit is not explained in the POB record.
risk_flags.mitigation: The draft preserves the differing capitalization without identifying them further.

spob_revision_history.previous_text: He says, “Listen now. Keep your body pure and undefiled. Then the spirit living in it can testify that your body is pure, and your body can be declared righteous. Never let yourself think, ‘My body will perish anyway,’ and use that as an excuse to defile it. If you defile your body, you will also defile the Holy Spirit. And if you defile your body, you will not live.”
spob_revision_history.review_summary: The draft usefully clarifies “flesh” as “body” and makes the warning against treating mortality as permission for defilement readily understandable. However, it makes the indwelling spirit’s otherwise unspecified testimony explicitly a testimony that the body is pure, despite the audit trail recognizing a broader live sense. It also shifts “may be justified” into “can be declared righteous.” Retain the testimony’s scope and the clause’s modal force while preserving the draft’s accessible body-language.

base_translation.text: “But if, Sir,” I say, “there has been some former ignorance before these words were heard, how will the man who has defiled his flesh be saved?”

translation.text: “But, sir,” I asked, “what if someone was ignorant before hearing these words? If that person has defiled their body, how can they be saved?”

simplification_decisions.pob_phrase: there has been some former ignorance before these words were heard
simplification_decisions.simplified_phrase: someone was ignorant before hearing these words
simplification_decisions.preserved_meaning: The person lacked this teaching before receiving it.
simplification_decisions.reasoning_layer_used: POB text and immediate sentence context
simplification_decisions.rationale: The direct wording removes an abstract construction without resolving what the ignorance involved.

simplification_decisions.pob_phrase: the man who has defiled his flesh
simplification_decisions.simplified_phrase: that person has defiled their body
simplification_decisions.preserved_meaning: The person has dishonored or polluted their own physical body.
simplification_decisions.rationale: “Body” communicates the physical sense of “flesh” clearly while retaining the image of defilement.

simplification_decisions.preserved_meaning: The speaker introduces a question addressed to “sir.”
simplification_decisions.rationale: “Asked” naturally identifies the speech as a question.

risk_flags.risk: “Defiled their body” may still leave the exact offense unspecified.
risk_flags.mitigation: The POB also leaves the offense unstated, so the draft preserves that restraint.

base_translation.text: “As to former ignorances,” he says, “God alone is able to give healing concerning them; for all authority is his. But now guard yourself, and the Lord, the Almighty—being full of compassion—will give healing for former ignorances, if from now on you do not defile your flesh or the spirit; for both are shared and cannot be defiled apart from one another. Therefore keep both pure, and you will live to God.”

translation.text: “As for your past ignorance,” he said, “God alone can heal you of it, because all authority belongs to him. But from now on, guard yourself. The Lord Almighty is full of compassion, and he will heal you of your past ignorance if you no longer defile your body or your spirit. They belong together, so you cannot defile one without defiling the other. Therefore, keep both pure, and you will live for God.”

simplification_decisions.preserved_meaning: God alone can remedy the person’s past ignorance.
simplification_decisions.rationale: The active wording is natural English while retaining the image of healing.

simplification_decisions.preserved_meaning: Both the physical and spiritual aspects of the person must remain pure.
simplification_decisions.rationale: “Body” makes the bodily sense of “flesh” clear without merging it with spirit.

simplification_decisions.pob_phrase: both are shared and cannot be defiled apart from one another
simplification_decisions.simplified_phrase: They belong together, so you cannot defile one without defiling the other
simplification_decisions.preserved_meaning: Body and spirit are joined, and defilement of either affects both.
simplification_decisions.rationale: The recast sentence states the same connection in ordinary English.

risk_flags.risk: “Ignorance” may include wrongs committed without knowledge, not merely lack of information.
risk_flags.mitigation: The main text retains POB’s broader term rather than narrowing it to sins.

risk_flags.risk: “Live for God” may sound mainly like a moral purpose rather than POB’s compressed “live to God.”
risk_flags.mitigation: The wording remains close to POB while using an intelligible English expression.

Ἄκουε νῦν, φησί· τὴν σάρκα σου ταύτην φύλασσε καθαρὰν καὶ ἀμίαντον, ἵνα τὸ πνεῦμα τὸ κατοικοῦν ἐν αὐτῇ μαρτυρήσῃ αὐτῇ, καὶ δικαιωθῇ σου ἡ σάρξ. 2. βλέπε μήποτε ἀναβῇ ἐπὶ τὴν καρδίαν σου τὴν σάρκα σου ταύτην φθαρτὴν εἶναι, καὶ παραχρήσῃ αὐτῇ ἐν μιασμῷ τινί. ἐὰν [γὰρ] μιάνῃς τὴν σάρκα σου, μιανεῖς καὶ τὸ πνεῦμα τὸ ἅγιον· ἐὰν δὲ μιάνῃς †τὴν σάρκα†, οὐ ζήσῃ. 3. Εἰ δέ τις, φημί, κύριε, γέγονεν ἄγνοια προτέρα πρὶν ἀκουσθῶσι τὰ ῥήματα ταῦτα, πῶς σωθῇ ὁ ἄνθρωπος ὁ μιάνας τὴν σάρκα αὐτοῦ; Περὶ τῶν προτέρων, φησίν, ἀγνοημάτων τῷ Θεῷ μόνῳ δυνατὸν ἴασιν δοῦναι· αὐτοῦ γάρ ἐστι πᾶσα ἐξουσία. 4. [ἀλλὰ νῦν φύλασσε σεαυτόν, καὶ ὁ Κύριος ὁ παντοκράτωρ, πολύσπλαγχνος ὤν, περὶ τῶν προτέρων ἀγνοημάτων ἴασιν δώσει,] ἐὰν τὸ λοιπὸν μὴ μιάνῃς σου τὴν σάρκα μηδὲ τὸ πνεῦμα· ἀμφότερα γὰρ κοινά ἐστι καὶ ἄτερ ἀλλήλων μιανθῆναι οὐ δύναται. ἀμφότερα οὖν καθαρὰ φύλασσε, καὶ ζήσῃ τῷ Θεῷ.
